matchdb is rebuilt when something it depends on changes, and each rebuild is
published as a new, separate release. This vignette covers:

* what triggers a rebuild;
* the steps from a new source file to a published reference;
* the checks a build must pass;
* what a user sees when a release lands.

If you only use the published references, read the last section.
`vignette("workspace")` covers updating your own downloaded copy.

## What triggers a rebuild

Three things change a build. They change different parts of it:

| what changed | example | what moves |
|---|---|---|
| **a source** | a new monthly BMF, a new tax year of e-file data | new observations; every count and table built from them |
| **the normalizer** | npnormalize 0.1.3 | the keys: every `*_derived` column, and everything built from the keys |
| **matchdb itself** | a fix to an ingest or a cluster rule | whatever that code builds |

A release is identified by what it was built from: the pinned source versions,
the matchdb commit, and the normalizer signature. All three are stamped on
everything published.

## 1. Pin the sources

Some upstream URLs are moving pointers (`latest/`). So no build reads them
directly. `dev/build-versions.R` names the version of every source a build
uses, in one place:

```{r}
V <- list(
  bmf_unified = "v2026-09-21",   # nccsdata unified BMF
  efile       = "v3_1",          # NCCS e-file, tax years 2009-2025
  e_postcard  = "v2026-07",
  ...)
```

`md_source_pin()` downloads each one into `sources/<source>/<version>/` and
writes a `PIN.dcf` beside it: the URL, the upstream modification time, the
size and the md5. Ingests read only the pinned copy, and the `source_vintage`
table records which pinned version each table was loaded from.
`md_source_moved()` reports when an upstream pointer has moved past its pin.
**A new source release is a new pin and a one-line change to
`dev/build-versions.R`.**

## 2. Fold the release into the ledger

Every name and address comes from the observation ledger: an append-only
table of every statement every source has made
(`vignette("corroboration-ledger")`). `md_build_ledger()` parses each pinned
file and applies it with `md_apply_release()`, one release per file. A
year-partitioned source is one release per tax year.

* **A file already applied is skipped,** by its md5. A new e-file version that
  re-releases only the latest two years touches only those two partitions.
* **What a release does depends on the kind of source** (`md_source_kinds()`):

  | kind | examples | a new release |
  |---|---|---|
  | `series`, `mentions` | 990 headers, Schedule I, Schedule R | statements not yet in the ledger are added; those still there are marked seen again; those the publisher dropped are marked `retracted_in` |
  | `snapshot` | the monthly BMF, the e-Postcard | compared with the values currently in force: a changed value closes one spell and opens another, and an EIN that drops off has its spell closed |
  | `cache` | the address crosswalk | diffed as a whole file; a new release is a correction |

  Snapshots must be applied in order; an older release than the newest one
  applied is refused.
* **Nothing is deleted.** A dissolved organization's names stay, with the
  dates they were in force. A snapshot source overwrites its own history
  upstream, so the ledger is the only place that history survives.

Two properties are tested for every source. **Applying the same release twice
changes nothing,** and **applying releases one at a time gives exactly the
ledger a rebuild from all the pins gives.** An incremental update cannot drift
from a clean build.

## 3. Rebuild everything downstream

Nothing downstream of the ledger is patched. It is rebuilt, deterministically,
in this order:

1. **Rollups:** `name` and `address`, with their counts (`n_corroborators`,
   `n_periods`, ...), from the whole ledger (`md_rollup()`). `former` names and
   which address is current are decided here too.
2. **Derived columns**, from `np_normalize()`: stored per distinct string and
   per normalizer signature (`name_text_derived`, `address_text_derived`), then
   linked to the rows (`md_link_derived()`). Only strings not seen before are
   normalized. A new monthly BMF adds a few thousand.
3. **Guards** on observed names (`md_guard_observed()`).
4. **Compact tables**, one row per `(ein, name_key)` and per address
   (`md_build_compact()`).
5. **Families and keys:** groups (`md_build_groups()`), places
   (`md_build_places()`), `ein_key` (`md_build_ein_key()`) and clusters
   (`md_build_clusters()`).
6. **Statistics cells** (`md_build_stats()`), which `md_compile()` sums.

Ids are content hashes, so a rebuild gives the same ids and nothing is
orphaned. `md_check_derived_fresh()` checks that every string has derived
columns for the installed signature.

**From scratch,** `dev/build-matchdb.R` pins every source, runs every ingest,
and builds all of the above in about 70 minutes, most of it deriving columns.
`dev/build-ledger.R --install` then builds the ledger and swaps the rollups
in. Every release so far was built this way, from scratch. The ledger is what
makes a release reproducible and diffable: it does not make a release
incremental yet.

## 4. A new normalizer

A new npnormalize signature changes keys, not observations. It is adopted on
a built database without rebuilding the ledger:

```{bash}
Rscript dev/rebuild-normalizer.R v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e             # derive beside the old, and report
Rscript dev/rebuild-normalizer.R v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e --install   # adopt it, rebuild downstream
Rscript dev/rebuild-normalizer.R v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e --drop-old  # once nothing published uses the old one
```

The first step stores the new signature's columns **beside** the old ones, so
nothing compile reads has changed yet. `md_normalizer_diff()` then reports what
would move: how many strings get a different value in each column, how many
compact groups merge or split, and how many EINs that touches.

For npnormalize 0.1.3 (2026-11-01), that report was:

* no name column moved, 0 of 12.8M `name` rows;
* of 12.99M address strings, 61,016 changed `street_unit`, 19,981 `street_num`,
  26,766 `street_name` and 6,921 `street_key`;
* on the `address` table, 6,068 of 22.0M rows rekeyed: 1,666 street-and-ZIP
  groups merged and 11 split, touching 1,593 EINs.

`--install` relinks the derived columns to the new signature and rebuilds
steps 3–6 above. `--drop-old` removes the old signature's columns only once
no published tier names it.

## 5. Check the build

A build can finish every step and still be wrong: a source that loaded one
year instead of ten, or a table built against stale ids. Before anything is
published, three checks run on the full database:

| check | script | passes when |
|---|---|---|
| **Phase 1 gate** | `dev/verify/run-gate.R` | the BMF-only reference matches a frozen baseline row for row and cell for cell, its statistics are identical, and a 1k benchmark gives identical results: three zeros |
| **Phase 2** | `dev/verify/phase2-measure.R` | adding observed names still gains what it gained before on the 1k benchmark (+146 YES at 2+ filers) |
| **build checks** | `dev/check-build.R` | every table exists and is non-empty, derived tables match the current ids, every EIN is known: 36 of 36 |

A new normalizer is *meant* to change the Phase 1 frame, so the baseline is
re-frozen under it (`dev/verify/build-baseline-2026-10.R`). Its benchmark
counts must not change. A gate that moves for a reason no one can explain
stops the release.

The 2026-11-01 release passed all three: three zeros against the re-frozen
baseline, Phase 2 +146 YES, and 36 of 36.

## 6. Publish

Publishing writes new files under new names. Nothing published is ever
overwritten.

1. **The four tiers** (`dev/verify/release/publish-tiers.R`): `md_publish()`
   compiles each spec and writes a bundle under `publish/<label>/<spec_hash>/`.
   The bundle holds the reference, its statistics, `addr_freq`, places and
   clusters, plus a `stamp.json` with md5s, the normalizer signature, and the
   matchdb and npnormalize versions.
2. **The tranches**: `md_publish_tranches()` writes the database as 108
   parquet files, split by table, layer and class, and a manifest. The
   build id is the date plus a hash of every file's md5
   (`2026-11-01-67c0bd2f`). Rows are written in a fixed order, so the same
   database gives the same files and the same id. A later build can then
   reuse every file that did not change.
3. **The tranche check** (`dev/verify/tranche-check.R`): each tier compiled
   from the tranches must be identical to its bundle.
4. **The databases** (`dev/verify/release/`): `compact.R` reclaims space,
   `slim.R` writes the user copy without the ledger, and `manifest.R` writes a
   `MANIFEST.json` for each, listing every pin.
5. **Upload** (`upload.sh`): files first, then manifests, and the
   `latest.json` pointers last. A reader never finds a pointer to a
   half-uploaded release.
6. **Fetch it back** (`verify-remote.R`, `dev/verify/tranche-remote.R`): over
   public HTTPS, with no credentials, as a user would. Every md5 must match,
   and what compiles must be identical to the bundles.

Old releases stay on S3 beside new ones. **Rolling back is editing a
pointer.**

## What a user sees

| you use | when a release lands |
|---|---|
| `md_reference("active-observed", fetch = "missing")` | nothing, until you fetch again: your local bundle is still the one you had. `md_fetch_reference()` gets the new one |
| `md_fetch_tranches(spec)` | `md_tranche_diff()` shows what changed, file by file; the next fetch copies the unchanged files and downloads the rest |
| `md_fetch_db()` | a new `MATCHDB.duckdb` and `MANIFEST.json` |

Two things protect results from a silent change:

* **The signature check.** Bundles and tranches built under one normalizer are
  refused under another. Query keys and reference keys must come from the
  same normalizer, or they disagree without any error. When npnormalize moves
  ahead of the published data, as 0.1.4 did on 2026-11-01, install the version
  the data was built with until it is rebuilt. `md_reference()`'s error names
  both signatures.
* **The workspace log.** Every fetch and compile records the build, the
  normalizer and the package versions. A `version_change` row marks every
  change (`md_log("version_change")`), so a match result can always be traced
  to the build and normalizer that produced it.

To reproduce an old result, pin all three packages and fetch the build you
used. Builds stay published, and their manifests name everything they were
made from.

## Releases so far

| date | normalizer | npnormalize | tranche build | what changed |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-26 | `v1-3e7b9f9d59bbb19e` | none (npmatch 0.1.1) | `2026-10-27-82c6f0cb` | first release from the ledger; the 0.1.1 tag |
| 2026-11-01 | `v1-592912060053c4c3` | 0.1.3 | `2026-11-01-67c0bd2f` | the new normalizer: unit precedence, whole-token house numbers, `BUILDING` as a unit; the same source data |

`NEWS.md` has the detail of each, and `dev/verify/logs/` keeps every log the
checks wrote.
